description.narrative: Our Voices Our Futures (OVOF) partners bring extensive experience of lobbying and advocacy at multiple levels to a range of issues connected to gender, sexuality and digital rights. OVOF partners ensure that ground-level evidence and lived realities of structurally silenced women feed directly into lobbying and advocacyat every level and international-level advocacy is translated back into community-level work in the six countries. More international and national-level law and policymakers need to acknowledge and address the issue of growing authoritarianism (and its impact on civic space, democracy and the lives of structurally silenced women) and the increasing influence of anti-gender and anti-rights actors within international and national policy and legal spaces. Key Dutch actors will be mobilised to collaborate with and support Women Human Rights Defenders, LBT activists and sex workers’ rights movements by creating and opening spaces for their participation in international processes such as the Commission on the Status of Women and the Human Rights Council so that their voices will be heard.

1. UHAI partner launched the first Intimate Partner Violence (IPV) training manual specifically tailored for the LGBTQI community. This pioneering resource equips GBV peer champions across different regions with the skills to identify, document, refer, and report IPV and GBV cases effectively. The manual marks a major step toward strengthening community-led responses to violence. To complement this effort, they plan to establish a dedicated helpline to offer direct support and guidance to survivors.The focus on agency building of community members by their peers has contributed to the amplification of voices of queer womxn in Uganda by highlighting their lived realities. 2. UHAI partner organised a leadership institute with 9 participants from 9 organisations, focusing on capacity building for LBQ women. This initiative provided training on various leadership skills, advocacy, and community mobilization, empowering participants to become effective leaders in their communities.
The target for this period is 1 advocacy action

FFP Panel titled “Transformative Approaches to Feminist Resourcing” : UHAI represented the OVOF Consortium in the panel discussion organised by the Count Me In! Consortium. Our contribution was focused on underpinning the need for more and better resourcing that sustains movements led by structurally silenced communities/women. UHAI specified the components of this resourcing as being: long term, flexible and sustained core support. We described our feminist value of approaching listening from a political perspective - listening is also a political act. Our contribution urged funders and allied partners to SSW/C movements to be deliberate about considering their political privilege and power when engaging with different voices and communities in the SSW/C movements - always asking “ who are the marginalised within the marginalised?” since SSW/C movements are not homogenous. We shared that funding should not perpetuate the already existing power dynamics. The nature of crisis in our region points to evidence showing that crisis does not happen in a vacuum - it is primarily orchestrated and sustained by political, economic and social structures. Our submission concluded by highlight in that while responding to safety and security needs of SSW/C communities is important, of even greater import is SSW/C movement building and sustenance of movement infrastructure.

1 submission and input by structurally silenced women in Uganda.

Negative attitudes and perceptions towards Structurally Silenced Women in Uganda have created an environment where members of the public are increasingly against communities of sexual and gender minorities and sex workers and their rights. This has not facilitated direct advocacy by our partners due to the underlying safety and security implications on UHAI's Structurally Silenced Women-led partners who prioritised strengthening partnerships with allies and Structurally Silenced Women's organisations instead as a way to progressively work towards greater engagement with mainstream Women's Rights organisations and feminist partners. Given the passing of the Anti-Homosexuality Bill in Uganda in early 2023, we anticipate some advocacy interventions by our partners (LBQT women and Female Sex Workers) in 2023.

UHAI supported and tracked 11 multi-level, cross-sectoral advocacy actions aimed at amplifying the agency and rights of LBTQ women, sex worker, trans and gender-diverse persons, and disabled queer persons in public space. These included formal dialogues with state institutions, health systems engagement, district-level planning processes, and legal recognition campaigns. Structurally silenced women (SSW) achieved greater visibility in public policy processes, with notable breakthroughs in state consultation, accountability mechanisms, and institutional commitments.

comment.narrative: In Uganda, the constitution is rather progressive and most of the legislation criminalising SSW, and making their organisations and activities difficult, is contradictory to the constitution. Other policies that need to improve are SSW’s right to own property, to education, to have a family regardless of your sexual orientation and gender identity, access to justice, the right for everyone to stand for election regardless of gender identity, as well as the registration of persons act that does not allow transgender and intersex persons to change name and gender marker.The details can be found in the baseline study.

1 initiative by structurally silenced women in Uganda that produces information material on the legal and policy framework governing digital technology and the rights of structurally silenced women.

Partner used magazine digital editions and online campaigns to call attention to online surveillance, disinformation, and tech-enabled exclusion of queer communities. Their digital media platforms served as tools for counter-surveillance narratives and engagement with digital rights communities working on tech justice. While not formal policy submissions, these campaigns shaped public discourse and supported civil society engagement on internet freedom and censorship.
